peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank all three Reviewers for their thorough, constructive, and highly insightful comments. We have now
performed a substantial set of new experiments, redone the RNA-seq under conditions that exac
tly match the liquid survival assays (no bacteria, liquid medium), introduced a properly c
ontrolled potassium-specific deficiency medium, and extensively reorganized and clarified
the manuscript. All changes are highlighted in red in the revised manuscript. A detailed Rep
orting Summary, Source Data file, and updated Data Availability statement are now provided.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Summary
This manuscript examines how potassium homeostasis influences immune responses and aging, primarily using
Caenorhabditis elegans, with additional studies in mouse myotube cells and yeast. The authors propose a mechanism
involving the p38–MAPK–ATF-7 axis, integrated with ASI neuronal signals, to promote survival under potassium deficiency.
The work suggests a broader link between ionic homeostasis, immune modulation, and strategies to combat antibiotic-
resistant pathogens. While potentially impactful and of broad interest, the manuscript has significant issues with
experimental design, interpretation, and presentation.
Response: We sincerely thank Reviewer #1 for the careful, detailed, and highly constructive
critique. We appreciate the Reviewer’s recognition that the study is “potentially impactful and of
broad interest.” The concerns raised have been extremely valuable in identifying critical
experimental gaps and presentation issues. We have addressed every major and minor point with
new data where required (including entirely new RNA-seq datasets under conditions identical to
the survival assays, properly controlled potassium-specific deficiency medium, quantification of
myotube formation, and many others), extensively reorganized the manuscript, and clarified all
interpretations. All changes are highlighted in the revised manuscript.
Major Points
1. The manuscript is dense, poorly organized, and sometimes lacks logical flow. Experiments and
interpretations are not always clearly described, making it difficult to read. Figures should be reorganized,
with some moved to supplementary materials or removed entirely if not essential. For example:
Response: We sincerely thank the Reviewer for highlighting the issues with density, organization,
and logical flow. In response, we closely follow the comments and carefully revised the manuscript
to clarify description of observation, interpret data more clearly, and reorganize figures.
Response: Thanks, we agree. As suggested, the schematic diagram of the p38–ATF-7 pathway
(former Fig. 1d) has been moved and is now presented as new Fig. 2a.
Fig. 2h–j adds little and could be removed.
Response: Thanks for this specific suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we have removed the
detailed schematic of the screening procedure (former Fig. 2h) to eliminate redundancy in the main
figures, while retained the screening results (former Fig. 2i,j) because it constitutes unbiased
forward-genetic evidence that loss of atf-7 function is the major suppressor of sek-1 lethality under
potassium deficiency (6/6 longest-surviving mutants carried independent atf-7 alleles). This
remains one of the strongest pieces of evidence that ATF-7 is the critical downstream effector of
p38 signaling in this context.
Fig. 7k could be simplified by removing redundant time points and instead quantifying proliferation and
myotube formation (see point 13).
Response: Thank you for this precise and constructive suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we
have removed the day 1 and day 3 time-course images from the main figure 7k. Instead, we now
provide rigorous and widely accepted quantitative readouts of myoblast differentiation that do not
rely on proliferation counting in confluent cultures. We quantified the length (Fig. 7l) and dimeter
(Fig. 7m) of myotubes per field after 4 days of differentiation with/without siRNA of Mapk14 or
Atp1a2 in C2C12 cells. As shown below, knockdown of Atp1a2 phenocopies p38α loss, confirming
that p38-mediated transcriptional upregulation of this Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase subunit is functionally
required for myogenic differentiation.
2. There are no direct data supporting coordination between tissues in response to low potassium, so this
conclusion cannot be made.
Response: Thanks for this important critique. We agree that identifying direct signals across
2
tissues would be perfect and further strengthen this conclusion. Nevertheless, our current data
provided evidence for inter-tissue coordination in response to low potassium.
We performed tissue-specific rescue of an upstream component of the p38 MAPK-CATP-3
axis, sek-1, in gene sek-1(km4) null mutant. Restoring sek-1 in ASI neurons significantly and
markedly extended lifespan under PD conditions compared with the sek-1 null mutant (Fig. 6b, c).
Although tissue-specific sek-1 RNAi experiments showed that knockdown in multiple tissues,
including ASI, significantly affected PD survival (Fig. 6f–j), the rescue experiments provided
additional insight into how tissues coordinate during PD survival.
As shown in Fig. 6d, intestine-specific rescue restored expression of immune genes; restoration
of sek-1 exclusively in the ASI fully rescued the dysregulated expression of the downstream target
catp-3 (Fig. 6d), which has been proved to mainly express and function in hypodermis — a distant
tissue from ASI (Fig. 5). Because sek-1 is not expressed in hypodermis but only in ASI under gpa-
4 promoter conditions, observed change in catp-3 mRNA level must be achieved via neuron-derived
signals acting on distal tissues. Therefore, the observation that restoring sek-1 only in ASI is
sufficient to normalize catp-3 expression in another tissue demonstrated functional inter-tissue
regulation in PD survival.
Together, these strengthened data demonstrate that potassium deficiency is sensed (at least in
part) by ASI neurons, which then transmit a non-cell-autonomous signal that transcriptionally
activates the critical potassium pump CATP-3 in the hypodermis. This establishes bona fide cross-
tissue coordination and justifies the conclusion that p38 orchestrates an organism-level response
to potassium scarcity.
3. The rationale for some experiments is unclear. For instance, phosphate buffer experiments in Fig. 1h–
j are poorly explained, and their purpose is ambiguous. Were they conducted to control for Cl- concentrations?
Response: We thank the Reviewer for pointing out the lack of clarity. In the revised manuscript,
we have completely rewritten this section and added new control experiments (potassium-free
NGM solution with CaCl₂ and MgSO₄) to make the rationale and interpretation explicit. The
purpose of the phosphate buffer experiments (Fig. 1h–j) was to rigorously exclude contributions
from anions (Cl⁻ vs. H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻), phosphate itself, buffering capacity, and pH, thereby
establishing that K⁺ is the sole cation required for survival of p38 pathway mutants under
potassium deficiency.
This conclusion can be underscored by direct pairwise comparisons (Fig. 1b–h; Extended
Data Fig. 1a). For mutant strains, survival of sek-1 and pmk-1 mutants dramatically changed
between 50 mM KPB and 50 mM SPB (19.4 d vs 5.2 d in sek-1 mutant; 29.6 d vs 10.8 d in pmk-1
mutant). In parallel, the difference between 50 mM KCl and 50 mM NaCl was also huge in both
sek-1 and pmk-1 mutants (18.5 d vs 1.6 d in sek-1 mutant; 25.8 d vs 4.7 d in pmk-1 mutant).
Meanwhile, survival differences between 50 mM KPB and 50 mM KCl, or between 50 mM SPB
and 50 mM NaCl were mirror.
In the revised manuscript, we edit and improve the text as “Collectively, these systematic
3
analyses demonstrate that survival of p38 pathway mutants under PD depends strictly and
specifically on extracellular K⁺. This requirement is independent of accompanying anions (Cl⁻ or
phosphate), phosphate itself, buffering capacity, pH, the presence of E. coli OP50-1, other cations
present in standard growth media (including Ca2+ and Mg2+), as well as culture format (liquid or
solid).”
4. The culture protocol departs from standard C. elegans methods but is insufficiently described. It is
unclear how worms survive with cholesterol as the only carbon source, whether they consume egg lysates,
and how FUDR is functioning in these conditions.
Response: For the liquid survival assays of in the method section, we have clearly described the
components of liquid medium as “Three days later, the day 3 adult animals were washed twice in
100 mM NaCl or the indicated solution and then transferred to individual wells of a 96-well
microplate containing 150 μL of 100 mM NaCl or the indicated solution, supplemented with 5 mg/L
cholesterol, 20 mg/L FUdR, and the antibiotic cocktail but without OP50-1.”
Energy source: the adult C. elegans can survive for days without any bacterial food, relying
entirely on their internal energy reserves. And the 5 µg/mL cholesterol is not used as the only
carbon/energy source, but serves only as an essential sterol for membrane synthesis (a requirement
that worms cannot meet de novo).
Role of FUdR: FUdR is included to prevent egg hatching so that there weren’t be newly
hatched larvae, thereby, ensuring that survival curves reflect only the lifespan of the original adult
cohort. FUdR can stop hatching because it can block thymidylate synthase in early embryos,
depriving them of thymidine triphosphate and causing replication-fork collapse within 2–3 cell
divisions; the resulting nuclear fragmentation lyses the developing cells inside the egg shell.
5. Lifespan experiments were done in liquid culture, while RNA-seq was performed on plate-grown
worms, introducing confounding variables. These experiments need to be conducted under the same
conditions.
Response: Thank you for this critical point and have fully addressed it. In the revised manuscript,
a new worm RNA-seq data have been performed with new datasets generated under conditions
identical to the liquid survival assays (no bacteria, liquid medium) for each wild type and pmk-1
mutant. For each strain, about 2,000 synchronized young adult worms were washed twice and
cultured for 4 hours under 20°C in either 100 mM NaCl or 100 mM KCl. The animals were then
collected for the RNA extraction and later RNA sequencing. The new liquid-condition
transcriptome perfectly recapitulates and strengthens the original findings (Fig. 3i–l; Extended
Data Fig. 3c, see below): 105 genes significantly upregulated by potassium deficiency in wild type
N2 worms (100 mM NaCl vs. 100 mM KCl, FDR < 0.05), including strong enrichment of
hypodermal genes, innate immune effectors, and catp-3 (PMK-1-dependent). The transcriptional
response described in the revised manuscript now directly reflects the physiological state
experienced during the survival assays, eliminating any confounding variables from solid agar,
live
bacteria, or developmental staging.
4
6. RNA-seq analysis is incomplete. C2C12 sequencing should include a 0 mM KCl condition, and worm
datasets should include mutants in the p38 pathway (e.g., sek-1).
Response: Thanks for this important comment. As described above, we have generated a new
RNA-seq in wild-type and pmk-1(km25) animals under identical liquid 100 mM NaCl vs. 100 mM
KCl conditions. These data demonstrate that potassium-deficiency induced catp-3 is p38-
dependent.
Because Mapk14-knockout C2C12 cells exhibit growth restriction under low-potassium
conditions, they cannot undergo normal differentiation assays. Moreover, both potassium ions and
the Mapk14 gene are indispensable for C2C12 myogenic differentiation; the absence of either factor
abolishes differentiation. Consequently, when wild-type and Mapk14-knockout C2C12 cells are
exposed to combinations of normal- and low-potassium conditions, only wild-type cells in a normal-
potassium environment are capable of differentiating, whereas the remaining three conditions fail
to support differentiation. Therefore, even if transcriptomic sequencing were performed under
these conditions, it would not allow meaningful analysis of the role of Mapk14 in C2C12
differentiation, nor would it illuminate the potassium-responsive mechanisms governed by Mapk14.
7. KCl rescues survival more effectively than NaCl but induces fewer transcriptional changes. This
discrepancy should be explained, possibly in terms of stress levels.
Response: Thanks for highlighting this important point. The apparent discrepancy is now
explicitly addressed in the revised manuscript. We fully understand that this apparent discrepancy
might seem puzzling, and the presentation in our original manuscript might contribute to this
5
impression. Indeed, conditions containing KCl (KCl alone or KCl rescue) provided environments
close to the standard one, and worms were not under strong stress. In contrast, worms in NaCl
experienced severe potassium-deficiency (PD) stress, resulting in significantly shortened lifespan
and transcriptional changes as adaptive responses to this adverse PD environment. Overall, long
lifespan and relatively few transcriptional changes observed in the KCl-rescued groups, compared
to the NaCl groups, directly reflects the severe stress imposed by potassium deprivation in the latter,
whereas KCl rescue restored the stress to a near-standard state and thereby alleviates the need for
a large-scale stress response. For better clarity, we have revised the relevant content to eliminate
any potential confusion or misunderstanding. We now state clearly: “The markedly fewer
transcriptional changes under KCl-replete conditions do not indicate lack of specificity; rather,
they reflect successful physiological rescue. Rapid restoration of K⁺ immediately corrects the
primary defect—disrupted ionic gradients and excitability—obviating the need for sustained
stress-responsive transcription. In contrast, NaCl-only conditions maintain lethal potassium
deficiency, driving a large-scale stress induced transcriptional program.”
8. The comparison in Fig. 2h between NaCl and NGM is not appropriate. Comparisons should instead
include KCl vs. NaCl and KCl vs. NGM (or water, if done in liquid culture).
Response: We thank the Reviewer for this comment. In Fig. 3h, we have included three pairwise
comparisons to address this concern: PD (100 mM NaCl) vs. high K⁺ (100 mM KCl), PD (100 mM
NaCl) vs. standard NGM, and high K⁺ (100 mM KCl) vs. standard NGM. These contrasts provide
a comprehensive and balanced evaluation of the effects of NaCl, KCl, and the NGM control.
9. WT worms survive better at acidic pH, while sek-1 mutants survive better at alkaline pH. This striking
result is not discussed.
Response: We appreciate the Reviewer for raising this point. However, the apparent “better”
survival of sek-1 mutants under alkaline conditions is observed only in the 0.1 M KCl condition
(15.4 d at pH 9.3 vs. 11.8 d at pH 4.3). As shown in Extended Data Table 1 (and summarized in the
supplemental table provided here), this difference is relatively small and is not consistently
observed across other ionic conditions. More importantly, the magnitude of this pH-dependent
variation is minor compared with the much more pronounced effect caused by the presence or
absence of potassium, which remains the dominant determinant of sek-1 mutant survival.
Therefore, this limited inconsistency does not affect the central conclusion of our study that
potassium availability is the predominant factor governing the survival of p38-pathway mutants.
10. Some data are inconsistent with the authors’ claims. For example:
• Fig. 5a: vhp-1 RNAi does not significantly change catp-3 expression.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for identifying this inaccuracy. In Fig. 5a, we used the
hypomorphic allele vhp-1(sa366). We acknowledge that this mutant does not significantly alter
catp-3 expression, and we have revised the text to accurately reflect this result. The revised sentence
in the main text now reads: “Consistent with prior findings, activation of the pathway by
overexpression of sek-1 and atf-7 strongly induced catp-3 mRNA, demonstrating that p38–ATF-7
signaling is sufficient for catp-3 transcriptional upregulation.”
• Fig. 5d–f: RNAi of catp-3 would have been more appropriate than stage-specific RNAi of sek-1 and
pmk-1.
Response: Thanks for this comment. The essential role of CATP-3 in PD survival has already been
rigorously demonstrated in Figures 3 and 4. Therefore, the experiments in Fig. 5d–h were designed
to address a different question—namely, how p38 signaling regulates catp-3 expression and PD
survival, rather than re-examining the effect of catp-3 depletion itself.
In Fig. 5d–h, stage-specific RNAi of sek-1 and pmk-1 allowed us to directly assess how
perturbing p38 signaling affects PD survival, as well as how reduced p38 activity (via sek-1 RNAi)
influences catp-3 expression. Using catp-3 RNAi in this context would only reiterate the established
requirement of CATP-3 for PD survival, without providing insights into the regulatory relationship
between the p38 pathway and catp-3.
Additionally, catp-3 RNAi is technically challenging: despite multiple attempts, we found that
catp-3 RNAi was ineffective for unknown reasons, and the high sequence similarity between catp-
3 and catp-2 (Extended Data Fig. 4d) makes it difficult to ensure target specificity and interpret
RNAi results with confidence. For these reasons, sek-1 and pmk-1 RNAi were the most appropriate
approaches for dissecting how p38 signaling modulates catp-3 expression and PD survival.
• Fig. 3j: Claims about lifespan, size, development, brood size, and pathogen resistance are not supported
by the figure.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for catching this oversight. We adjust our description in the
main text. “The catp-3 mutant was highly sensitive to PD, showing significantly reduced survival
at potassium levels below 5 mM (Fig. 3i), yet exhibited wild type lifespan and pathogen resistance
under standard conditions (Fig. 3j and Extended Data Fig. 3j).”
11. C2C12 myotube formation and proliferation need to be quantified.
Response: Thank you for this precise and constructive suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we
have removed the Day 1 and Day 3 time-course images from the main Fig. 7k. Instead, we now
7
provide rigorous and widely accepted quantitative measurements of C2C12 differentiation that do
not depend on proliferation counts in confluent cultures. Specifically, after 4 days of differentiation
with or without siMapk14 or siAtp1a2, we quantified two standard morphological indicators of
myogenic maturation: myotube length (Fig. 7l) and myotube diameter (Fig. 7m) per field. These
quantitative analyses demonstrate that Atp1a2 knockdown phenocopies p38α loss, supporting the
conclusion that p38α-dependent transcriptional upregulation of this Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase subunit is
functionally required for proper myotube formation.
12. The effects of atf-7 mutants are shown, but it is not explained how the point mutations affect ATF-7
function.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for pointing out the need to clarify how the atf-7 point mutations
affect ATF-7 function. We have added a detailed explanation of all atf-7 alleles used in the Figure
2j legend in revised manuscript. Summary of allele effects (now explicitly stated):
atf-7(qd22gf): Prevents relieving of repressive activity → acts as a constitutive repressor
(Shivers et al., PLoS Genet 2010).
Loss-of-function alleles identified in our suppressor screen:
ld09: GAA→TAA premature stop codon → truncation lacking the entire bZIP DNA-binding
and dimerization domain → predicted null.
ld18 (qd137): established strong loss-of-function allele (a deletion in exon 4).
ld37: 158-bp deletion removing most of the bZIP domain.

13. The upregulation of catp-3 in NaCl versus KCl needs functional interpretation.
Response: Thank you for this comment. We have added a clear functional interpretation in the
revised manuscript. The strong induction of catp-3 specifically under potassium deficiency (100
mM NaCl) represents a physiologically appropriate compensatory response: severe extracellular
K⁺ depletion collapses the K⁺ gradient, depolarizes excitable tissues, and triggers lethal muscle
spasms and neuronal dysfunction (Fig. 1k, Supplementary Videos). Upregulation of the
hypodermal Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase CATP-3 increases pump density, thereby enhancing K⁺ reuptake
capacity into the animal. Because the hypodermis is the major non-excitable epithelial barrier in
C. elegans and directly contacts pseudocoelomic fluid and muscles, elevated hypodermal CATP-3
likely restores organismal K⁺ homeostasis by: re-establishing trans-hypodermal K⁺ transport;
repolarizing adjacent muscle and neurons indirectly; preventing catastrophic ion leakage and
volume dysregulation.
In contrast, KCl-replete conditions (100 mM KCl) maintain normal extracellular K⁺,
eliminating the need for compensatory pump upregulation—hence catp-3 expression remains basal.
This is directly analogous to the well-documented upregulation of renal Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase α1 and β1
8
subunits during dietary or pathological potassium deficiency in mammals.

This manuscript presents interesting findings showing that the p38 MAPK–ATF-7 pathway orchestrates
cross-tissue potassium homeostasis for organismal survival under potassium deficiency (PD). The
authors demonstrate that ASI sensory neurons communicate with the hypodermis in C. elegans and
extend their observations to mammalian and yeast systems. Mutant worms with disruptions in the p38
MAPK pathway exhibited markedly reduced survival in water lacking salts or nutrients. Supplementation
with potassium chloride (KCl), but not sodium chloride (NaCl), rescued the sensitivity of these
mutants, suggesting that the pathway is critical when potassium is limiting. An EMS suppressor screen further
identified ATF-7, a downstream transcription factor of p38 MAPK, as an important regulator of
potassium homeostasis. RNA-seq analysis also revealed CATP-3, a P-type ATPase, as a functional
downstream target. Together, these data provide potentially novel insights into the molecular mechanisms
of potassium homeostasis across species.
Response: We thank Reviewer #2 for the thoughtful and constructive evaluation of our work. We
are pleased that the reviewer finds the study interesting and recognizes the significance of our
findings on the p38 MAPK–ATF-7 pathway in orchestrating cross-tissue potassium homeostasis
and promoting organismal survival under potassium deficiency. We appreciate the positive
assessment of our genetic, physiological, and cross-species analyses, and we are encouraged that
the reviewer considers our insights into CATP-3/P-type ATPase regulation and conserved
potassium homeostasis mechanisms to be potentially novel and valuable. We have carefully
addressed all specific comments point-by-point in the responses below and have revised the
manuscript accordingly to improve clarity, rigor, and overall presentation.
Major Comments
1. The standard nematode growth medium (NGM) contains peptone, cholesterol, NaCl, CaCl2, MgSO4,
and potassium phosphate buffer, which are essential for worm growth and survival. The authors describe
PD conditions as water supplemented with NaCl. However, this medium lacks many NGM components
and is not specifically deficient only for potassium. The absence of other essential nutrients complicates
the interpretation. A true PD condition should include all other NGM components except potassium.
This limitation should be addressed directly.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for this important and well-taken comment. We agree that the
standard nematode growth medium (NGM) contains multiple essential components, and that a
medium lacking these constituents cannot be considered exclusively potassium-deficient. In our
original experiments, the “PD medium” was intentionally simplified to a 0.1 M NaCl aqueous
solution to isolate ionic effects. Empirically, we found that inclusion of other NGM components in
this simplified system produced only minimal changes in survival compared to 0.1 M NaCl alone,
which initially justified the use of this condition. Nonetheless, we fully acknowledge that the
absence of a potassium-free NGM control represented a limitation of the original study design.
To address this concern directly, we have now performed additional lifespan assays using a
potassium-free NGM formulation that retains all other essential NGM components. This
potassium-free NGM contained 100 mM NaCl, 25 mM sodium phosphate buffer (SPB; 2.38 g/L
100 mg/L FUdR, and the same antibiotic cocktail used in all other experiments. These new data
are presented in Extended Data Fig. 1d. In addition, we have included results from a solid-plate
PD assay (Extended Data Fig. 1c) to exclude potential artifacts associated with liquid culture.
Across these conditions, p38 pathway mutants displayed markedly reduced survival in the
absence of extracellular potassium, and this defect was robustly rescued by K⁺ supplementation.
Importantly, this requirement for potassium was independent of accompanying anions (Cl⁻ versus
phosphate), buffering capacity, pH, the presence of E. coli OP50-1, other divalent cations present
in standard growth media (including Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺), and culture format (liquid versus solid).
Together, these systematic analyses demonstrate that the survival defect observed under PD
conditions reflects a specific requirement for extracellular K⁺, rather than the absence of other
essential NGM components.
2. KCl supplementation substantially increased survival in both wild-type and sek-1 (and pmk-1) mutants,
with a stronger effect on the mutants. However, the magnitude of this effect raises the possibility of non-
specific lifespan extension by KCl. The specificity of this rescue should be clarified. In particular, the
effects of other salts such as CaCl2 and MgSO4 should be examined or discussed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the specificity of the
KCl-mediated rescue. To address the possibility that the observed lifespan extension reflects a non-
specific salt or osmotic effect, we performed additional control experiments using other salts.
Supplementation with CaCl₂ or the potassium-free NGM solution under otherwise identical
conditions produced only minor or no improvement in survival in either wild-type or sek-1/pmk-1
mutant animals, and the magnitude of these effects was substantially smaller than that observed
with KCl. Moreover, these salts failed to preferentially rescue the shortened survival of the p38
pathway mutants. Together, these results indicate that the survival benefit is not a general
consequence of increased ionic strength or salt supplementation, but is largely specific to K⁺. This
specificity is consistent with our model that potassium availability acts as a physiologically relevant
signal that engages p38 MAPK–dependent protective responses, rather than causing non-specific
lifespan extension.
3. Line 59: “Initially, wild type (N2) worms in water without salt supplementation exhibited a mean
lifespan of approximately 19 days, comparable to that on standard nematode growth medium (NGM)
13
plates with live OP50-1 (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1a and Extended Data Table 1)13, indicating normal
aging without significant stress under baseline conditions.” I disagree with this interpretation. The
reported 19-day lifespan cannot be regarded as “normal aging without significant stress.” Instead, it likely
represents a composite outcome of two opposing influences: lifespan extension due to food
deprivation (T. L. Kaeberlein et al., Aging Cell 5, 487–494 (2006); G. D. Lee et al., Aging Cell 5, 515–524 (2006))
and a detrimental effect caused by salt deprivation. This sentence should therefore be rewritten to avoid
implying physiological normalcy under such conditions.
Moreover, as this condition forms the foundation of the experimental paradigm used throughout the study,
the interpretation of all subsequent results requires careful reconsideration. For instance, the shortened
lifespan of p38 MAPK mutants in water could be at least partly due to the established requirement of
p38 MAPK signaling for lifespan extension under food deprivation (a form of dietary restriction in C.
elegans). This possibility should be experimentally tested through additional rigorous control
experiments and discussed thoroughly in the revised manuscript.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for this careful and important critique. We fully agree that
describing the lifespan of wild-type worms in water as reflecting “normal aging without significant
stress” was inappropriate, and we regret the imprecise wording. Our original intent was not to
imply physiological normalcy, but rather to note that the net lifespan outcome under this condition
happened to be numerically comparable to that observed on standard NGM plates with live OP50-
1. We now recognize that this comparison was conceptually misleading.
As the Reviewer correctly points out, lifespan in water likely reflects the combined influence
of at least two opposing factors: lifespan extension due to bacterial food deprivation (dietary
restriction)14–16 and lifespan shortening caused by deprivation of essential salts and ions. We have
therefore revised the text to remove any implication of “normal aging” and to explicitly
acknowledge this composite effect.
The revised sentence now reads: “Initially, wild type (N2) worms in water without salt
supplementation exhibited a mean lifespan of approximately 19 days, comparable to that on
standard nematode growth medium (NGM) plates with live OP50-1 (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig.
1a and Extended Data Table 1)13. This observed lifespan likely reflects the net effect of two
counteracting factors: prolongation arising from bacterial food deprivation14-16 and a
countervailing shortening induced by the absence of essential salts.”
We also agree that this issue has important implications for interpretation of the shortened
lifespan observed in p38 MAPK pathway mutants. p38 signaling has indeed been implicated in
lifespan extension under dietary restriction–like conditions in C. elegans, raising the possibility
that the reduced survival of these mutants in water may partially reflect impaired adaptation to
food deprivation rather than salt deprivation alone.
To address this concern, we have expanded the experimental framework and discussion in the
revised manuscript. Specifically, we now (i) include potassium-deficient but otherwise complete
NGM conditions (Extended Data Fig. 1d), (ii) perform survival assays on solid media with defined
salt composition while maintaining equivalent dietary inputs (Extended Data Fig. 1c), and (iii)
directly compare conditions that differ in potassium availability while maintaining equivalent ionic
14
inputs (Extended Data Fig. 1a). These analyses demonstrate that loss of p38 pathway function leads
to a selective vulnerability to potassium deprivation that cannot be explained solely by altered
responses to food deprivation. We have also revised the Discussion to explicitly acknowledge the
interaction between dietary restriction and ionic stress and to clarify the boundaries of our
experimental paradigm.

This study, "p38 MAPK orchestrates cross-tissue potassium homeostasis for survival," uncovers a
previously uncharacterized role for p38/MAPK signaling in promoting survival during potassium
deficiency (PD) in C. elegans. The authors present convincing evidence that this pathway functions
through hypodermal upregulation of CATP-3, a P-type ATPase potassium pump, and integrates both
neuronal and peripheral signaling. They further extend their findings to mammalian cell lines and yeast
models, demonstrating the conserved role of p38/MAPK-mediated regulation of P-type ATPases.
Overall, the study is novel, the data are well supported, and the manuscript is clearly written and well organized.
There are some considerations, listed below, that should be addressed for clarity and to rule out
alternative hypotheses.
Response: We thank Reviewer #3 for the positive and thoughtful evaluation of our work. We
appreciate the recognition of the novelty, clarity, and broad relevance of our study, and we are
grateful for the constructive suggestions provided. We have carefully addressed each of the points
raised by the Reviewer, as detailed below, and have revised the manuscript accordingly to improve
clarity and strengthen our conclusions.
Items to address:
1. Fasting is known to activate p38/MAPK signaling. It would be informative to test whether KCl
supplementation triggers fed-like signaling or suppresses the fasting response in the worms.
Response: We fully agree with the Reviewer that this is an important and intriguing question.
Feeding and fasting states are associated with distinct signaling pathways and physiological
responses in C. elegans, commonly assessed by IIS activity (e.g., DAF-16 localization and target
gene expression), AMPK phosphorylation, and autophagy levels. p38/MAPK signaling has also
been reported to respond to nutritional status; however, its regulation is highly time-dependent.
Short-term fasting can suppress p38 activity, whereas prolonged fasting may activate p38, while
long-term dietary restriction has been reported to reduce p38 signaling. Thus, the relationship
between p38 activity and feeding/fasting reflects complex, time-course–dependent changes.
In addition, p38 signaling responses to both nutritional cues and potassium deprivation (PD)
are often context- and tissue-specific. As requested, we transferred day-1 adult wild-type worms to
liquid PD conditions (0.1 M NaCl) with OP50-1 for 24 hours, followed by supplementation with
100 mM KCl for either 4 hours or 24 hours. qPCR analysis showed that sysm-1 (a feeding-
upregulated gene and a known p38/ATF-7 downstream target) as well as catp-3 mRNA levels were
suppressed upon KCl supplementation at both time points.
These results suggest that KCl supplementation might not simply restore a canonical feeding-
like transcriptional program, but rather modulate p38-dependent signaling in a distinct manner.
Whether KCl suppresses specific fasting-associated responses or induces a fed-like signaling state
through p38 remains an interesting and complex question that warrants further systematic
investigation.

2. Pharyngeal pumping in C. elegans relies on Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity. How do the conditions used in
this manucript (e.g., PD and KCl supplementation) affect pharyngeal pumping behavior?
Response: We appreciate the Reviewer’s thoughtful question. Pharyngeal pumping is primarily
driven by MC/M3 motor neurons and requires the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase EAT-6. Several lines of evidence
indicate that the PD and KCl conditions used in our study do not confound our findings through
altered pumping behavior. First, the key genetic manipulations that produced strong phenotypes—
such as ASI-specific sek-1 rescue or ASI-specific RNAi—target neurons that are not involved in
pharyngeal pumping, making pumping-rate changes an unlikely explanation. Second, catp-3
expression and functional requirement are localized to the hypodermis rather than the pharynx,
further reducing the likelihood that altered pumping underlies the observed survival effects.
Finally, worms under short-term PD (20 h), the window in which transcriptional measurements
were taken, do not display overt defects in feeding or pharyngeal movement. Together, these points
support that the PD survival phenotypes and transcriptional changes we report are not
attributable to changes in pharyngeal pumping.

rescues survival only when applied within a short time window after transfer to PD conditions,
indicating that the protective p38-dependent response must be activated early. This temporal

compared short (4 h) and prolonged (24 h) KCl supplementation following PD. As described above,
extending KCl treatment from 4 to 24 hours did not result in substantial additional changes,

sensitivity. We speculate that brief PD followed by rapid KCl repletion may allow partial

datasets under exactly the same conditions as the survival assays—liquid medium, no bacteria, and
matched NaCl/KCl treatments. For each genotype (N2 and pmk-1), ~2,000 synchronized young
adults were exposed for 4 hours to either 100 mM NaCl or 100 mM KCl before RNA extraction.

worms, including hypodermal genes, innate immune effectors, and catp-3, all showing clear PMK-

or without bacteria.

potassium deprivation and does not affect the essential role of the p38 pathway in promoting

mutants under water conditions (Extended Data Fig. 1b), further supporting the idea that p38
signaling is particularly required for survival under conditions of limited exogenous K+, rather

Response: To directly test whether KCl supplementation suppresses the fasting response or induces
a fed-like signaling state, we measured the expression of established fasting-responsive genes in C.
elegans. Specifically, we analyzed lgg-1 (autophagy-related), atgl-1 (lipolysis), sod-3 (a canonical

conditions with OP50-1 for 24 hours, followed by supplementation with 100 mM KCl for either 4
hours or 24 hours. Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that the expression levels of these four
fasting-responsive genes showed no significant changes upon KCl supplementation at either time
point, under liquid conditions with or without food.

differential expression of lgg-1, atgl-1, sod-3, or pha-4 between 0.1 M NaCl and 0.1 M KCl

transcriptional program nor induce a fed-like signaling state, arguing against the possibility that

signaling.

conditions to rule out altered feeding behavior as a confounding factor? This is a very easy question to

measured pharyngeal pumping rates under the same liquid survival conditions used in the
manuscript. Young adult worms were transferred to liquid medium without food containing either
0.1 M NaCl (PD) or 0.1 M KCl for 24 hours, and pumping rates were quantified thereafter. Under
these conditions, PD exposure did not significantly alter pharyngeal pumping rates in wild-type
worms, indicating that potassium deficiency per se does not impair pumping behavior in a normal
genetic background. In contrast, pmk-1 mutants exhibited a significant reduction in pumping rates
under PD, suggesting reduced physiological activity or stress sensitivity specific to this genotype.

heterogeneous than those typically observed on food-containing solid plates, with individual
animals showing variable pumping frequencies. This pattern closely resembles previously
described starvation-induced pumping behavior on solid media, indicating that the liquid
environment itself does not uniquely suppress pharyngeal activity beyond the expected effects of
fasting. Together, these data demonstrate that neither PD exposure nor KCl supplementation alters
pharyngeal pumping in wild-type worms, and therefore altered feeding behavior is unlikely to
account for the observed survival phenotypes.

wild-type worms to liquid PD conditions (0.1 M NaCl) with OP50-1 for 24 hours, followed by
supplementation with 100 mM KCl for either 4 hours or 24 hours. qPCR analysis showed that sysm-1 (a

directly attributable to KCl supplementation.
Response: To clarify whether p38/MAPK signaling is dynamically regulated during PD exposure
and KCl supplementation, or instead constitutively required for survival, we examined the
expression of two well-established p38/PMK-1 downstream target genes: sysm-1 (feeding- and
pathogen-induced) and catp-3 (PD-induced). Young adult wild-type worms were transferred to
liquid potassium-deficient (PD; 0.1 M NaCl) conditions for 24 hours, followed by supplementation
with 100 mM KCl for either 4 hours or 24 hours. To explicitly address the reviewer’s concern
regarding food effects, these experiments were performed both in the presence and absence of
OP50-1.
Under liquid conditions with food, sysm-1 expression was not strongly induced by PD and was
modestly suppressed upon KCl supplementation at 4 hours, with no further suppression at 24
hours. In contrast, catp-3 expression increased progressively with prolonged PD exposure and was
significantly suppressed by KCl supplementation at 4 hours, with further reduction at 24 hours.

PD or KCl supplementation, consistent with the known dependence of sysm-1 on feeding cues. This
observation is in agreement with our RNA-seq data, in which sysm-1 was not induced by PD in
liquid culture without food, but was induced under PD conditions on solid plates with food (Fig. 3).

and was robustly suppressed by KCl supplementation.

induced by PD, and that their regulation is highly context-dependent. While sysm-1 responds
primarily to feeding status, catp-3 is selectively sensitive to potassium availability, showing dynamic

findings support a model in which p38/MAPK signaling is required for survival under PD but is
not globally activated as a canonical stress response, with potassium-sensitive regulation acting on
a subset of p38 downstream targets such as catp-3.

Young adult wild-type worms were transferred to liquid potassium-deficient (PD; 0.1 M NaCl)
conditions with OP50-1 for 24 hours, followed by supplementation with 100 mM KCl for either 4
hours or 24 hours. Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that the expression levels of these four
fasting-responsive genes showed no significant changes upon KCl supplementation at either time

Consistent with these results, analysis of our RNA-seq datasets likewise showed no significant

transcriptional program nor induce a fed-like signaling state, arguing against the possibility that

these conditions, PD exposure did not significantly alter pharyngeal pumping rates in wild-type
worms, indicating that potassium deficiency per se does not impair pumping behavior in a normal
genetic background. In contrast, pmk-1 mutants exhibited a significant reduction in pumping rates
under PD, suggesting reduced physiological activity or stress sensitivity specific to this genotype.
Notably, under liquid fasting conditions, overall pumping rates were lower and more
heterogeneous than those typically observed on food-containing solid plates, with individual
animals showing variable pumping frequencies. This pattern closely resembles previously
described starvation-induced pumping behavior on solid media, indicating that the liquid
environment itself does not uniquely suppress pharyngeal activity beyond the expected effects of
fasting. Together, these data demonstrate that neither PD exposure nor KCl supplementation alters
pharyngeal pumping in wild-type worms, and therefore altered feeding behavior is unlikely to
account for the observed survival phenotypes.

supplementation with 100 mM KCl for either 4 hours or 24 hours. qPCR analysis showed that sysm-1 (a

Response: To clarify whether p38/MAPK signaling is dynamically regulated during PD exposure
and KCl supplementation, or instead constitutively required for survival, we examined the
expression of two well-established p38/PMK-1 downstream target genes: sysm-1 (feeding- and
pathogen-induced) and catp-3 (PD-induced). Young adult wild-type worms were transferred to
liquid potassium-deficient (PD; 0.1 M NaCl) conditions for 24 hours, followed by supplementation
with 100 mM KCl for either 4 hours or 24 hours. To explicitly address the reviewer’s concern
regarding food effects, these experiments were performed both in the presence and absence of
OP50-1.
Under liquid conditions with food, sysm-1 expression was not strongly induced by PD and was
modestly suppressed upon KCl supplementation at 4 hours, with no further suppression at 24
hours. In contrast, catp-3 expression increased progressively with prolonged PD exposure and was
significantly suppressed by KCl supplementation at 4 hours, with further reduction at 24 hours.
Under liquid conditions without food, sysm-1 expression was low and not responsive to either
PD or KCl supplementation, consistent with the known dependence of sysm-1 on feeding cues. This

Together, these data indicate that p38/MAPK target genes are not uniformly or globally
induced by PD, and that their regulation is highly context-dependent. While sysm-1 responds
primarily to feeding status, catp-3 is selectively sensitive to potassium availability, showing dynamic

induction by PD and rapid repression upon KCl supplementation regardless of food. These
findings support a model in which p38/MAPK signaling is required for survival under PD but is
not globally activated as a canonical stress response, with potassium-sensitive regulation acting on
a subset of p38 downstream targets such as catp-3.
